title: Why do I compare myself to everyone? What helps when you feel behind in life
description: Why comparison is automatic when no objective yardstick exists, why the same success can inspire or deflate depending on relevance and attainability, why passive feeds carry the cost — and what helps in order: name the comparison, cut passive looking, test the target, extract one copyable step, and keep one fair comparison against your own record.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

Someone your age posts a promotion. A friend posts a new home, a new body, a book deal, a child, a start-up. You were fine a minute ago. Now your own life looks late, small and badly managed, and you keep returning to the post as if looking again will tell you where you stand. If you have searched "why do I compare myself to everyone" or "how do I stop feeling behind in life", this guide is for that moment. It sets out what the research actually shows about why comparison is automatic, why it sometimes inspires and sometimes deflates, what helps in the order most people can use it, and where an app fits — including ours, with our measured numbers printed as they are.

We are Anicca. We make a small affirmation app, and overthinking and a hard day are among the struggles people can choose inside it. This guide is not an ad and it is not treatment. Comparing yourself to others is not, by itself, a diagnosis.

## Why do I keep comparing myself to other people?

Comparison is not a character flaw you opted into. Four findings explain most of its force.

**First, when there is no objective yardstick, other people become the yardstick.** Festinger (1954) proposed that people have a drive to evaluate their opinions and abilities, and that when objective, non-social means are not available, they evaluate themselves by comparison with others. He also proposed that the tendency to compare with a given person falls as the difference between you grows — we compare most with people who feel close enough to be relevant. That is why a stranger's lottery win barely registers and a former classmate's promotion can ruin an evening. "Am I doing well?" has no objective scale. A peer's post supplies one, instantly, and not a fair one.

**Second, some people compare more often and feel it more strongly, and that tendency is measurable.** Gibbons and Buunk (1999) built the Iowa–Netherlands Comparison Orientation Measure (INCOM), an 11-item scale developed and validated in several thousand people in each of the United States and the Netherlands. People high in comparison orientation sought out more comparisons, spent more time on them and felt them more strongly, and they tended to score higher in self-consciousness and negative affectivity and somewhat lower in self-esteem. The point is practical, not labelling: if comparison hits you harder than it hits the person next to you, that is a known individual difference, not evidence that your life is actually worse.

**Third, upward comparison can go either way — contrast or assimilation — and attainability helps decide which.** In her review, Collins (1996) argued that comparing upward, to someone doing better, can lower your self-evaluation by contrast ("I am far behind") or raise it by assimilation ("I am like them, so that future is partly mine"), depending in part on whether you expect similarity to the target. Lockwood and Kunda (1997), in work titled "Superstars and me", showed the same split for role models: an outstanding person inspired people when their success seemed relevant to the self and attainable, and deflated people when the same kind of success seemed out of reach. The post is the same. The verdict changes with one question your mind answers before you notice it: "could that be me, by a path I can actually take?"

**Fourth, feeds industrialised the upward direction, and the average effect is negative and small — not zero, and not destiny.** McComb, Vanman and Tobin (2023) combined 48 experimental articles involving 7,679 participants and 118 effect sizes. Exposure to upward comparison targets on social media produced an overall negative effect on self-evaluations and emotions (g = −0.24), with negative effects on body image (g = −0.31), subjective well-being (g = −0.19), mental health (g = −0.21) and self-esteem (g = −0.21). Vogel and colleagues (2014) found the same pattern in two studies: people who used Facebook most often had poorer trait self-esteem, mediated by greater exposure to upward comparisons, and in an experiment, state self-esteem and relative self-evaluations were lower after viewing an upward-comparison profile than after a downward-comparison one. Steers, Wickham and Acitelli (2014) named the mechanism in their title — seeing everyone else's highlight reels: in Study 1 (N = 180), time on Facebook was associated with depressive symptoms, and in Study 2, a 14-day diary study (N = 152), Facebook social comparisons mediated the link between time and logins and depressive symptoms. These are associations and short-term experiments, mostly in young adults on one platform. They do not prove that a feed caused anyone's depression. They do show that the comparison your mind makes from a highlight reel is built from selected evidence, and that treating it as a full report is a measurement error.

There is one more link worth knowing, because it connects this guide to the night hours. Feinstein and colleagues (2013) followed 268 college-age young adults over 3 weeks and found that negatively comparing yourself to others on Facebook predicted increases in rumination, which in turn were associated with increases in depressive symptoms — and this held over and above a general tendency to compare. The comparison ends in a minute. The rumination it starts can run for hours.

## What helps, in the order most people can use it

You will not stop comparing. Festinger's (1954) account says the drive to evaluate is basic, and Gibbons and Buunk (1999) show its strength varies by person, not by willpower sermon. What can change is the target, the dose, the direction of the information, and what you do in the five minutes after.

### 1. Name the comparison in one sentence — target, dimension, missing information

When the sting arrives, write one sentence with three parts: who you compared with, on which single dimension (money, body, career, love, speed), and what you do not actually know about their situation. ("I compared my whole career with her promotion post. I do not know her hours, her debts, her help, or what she gave up.") This is not positive thinking. It is correcting the sample. Steers and colleagues' (2014) highlight-reel finding is that the input was selected — the best moments, edited — while your side of the comparison is unedited, including the parts nobody posts. Naming the missing information does not make the other person's success smaller. It makes your measurement honest about what it was made from.

### 2. Cut passive looking first — before you try to think differently

The strongest experimental lever in this literature is not a mindset. It is the mode of use. Verduyn and colleagues (2015) ran two studies. In Study 1, 84 undergraduates were cued to use Facebook passively — scrolling and looking without interacting — rather than actively, and passive use led to declines in affective well-being over the day. Study 2 used experience sampling in daily life and found the same pattern, with envy as the mechanism: passive use predicted increases in envy, which predicted declines in how people felt, while active use did not show that pattern. So for one week, change the mode before you change your mind: mute or unfollow the accounts that reliably sting, open a feed only when you are looking for something specific, and when you do open it, do one active thing — send the message, answer the person — and close it. You are not quitting the internet. You are removing the exact condition the experiment isolated.

### 3. Ask the two questions that decide whether a comparison can help — is it relevant, and is it attainable?

Lockwood and Kunda (1997) give you a test with two parts. First: is this dimension actually one of your goals, in your life as it is — or did the feed assign it to you in the last thirty seconds? A comparison on a dimension you never chose is information about someone else's life, not about yours. Second: is there a version of that outcome that is attainable for you, by steps that exist? If the answer to both is yes, keep the comparison — Step 4 uses it. If either answer is no, the research predicts the comparison will mostly deflate, and the honest move is to retire that target: unfollow, mute, or deliberately reclassify the post as news about them, not a measurement of you. Retiring a target is not sour grapes. Collins (1996) is clear that the same upward target produces opposite effects depending on how it is construed; choosing the construal is the skill.

### 4. If it passes both questions, extract exactly one copyable step — and let envy point at it

Envy is painful, but it is not all one thing. Van de Ven, Zeelenberg and Pieters (2009) showed empirically that benign envy — the kind aimed at improving your own position — is a different experience from malicious envy, which aims at pulling the other person down. In later work, Van de Ven and colleagues (2011) found across four studies that benign envy, not admiration and not malicious envy, motivated people to improve themselves, and that an upward comparison triggered benign envy and better performance only when people thought self-improvement was attainable — which is why this step comes after Step 3, not before it. The practice is small: from the person's story, take exactly one thing they did that you can copy this week — the course, the portfolio page, the morning hour, the application sent — write it as a next step with a time, and stop there. Do not copy their whole life plan in an evening. One step converts the comparison from a verdict into information. If you cannot find a copyable step, the comparison failed Step 3 and belongs back there.

### 5. Keep one comparison that is fair — you, against your own record

Festinger (1954) put objective means first: when an objective standard exists, people do not need a social one. Your own record is the closest fair standard you have, because it holds the starting point, the constraints and the costs constant. Once a week, in writing, note one dimension you actually chose and where it stands against your own record from three months ago — from notes, photos, accounts or a calendar, not from memory, because memory edits in the same direction feeds do. Some weeks the record will show no movement, and that is real information too: it points at the step, the help or the rest that is missing, not at another person's timeline. This is also the comparison to use at night, when Feinstein and colleagues' (2013) rumination link is strongest in practice: replace "where is she?" with "what is one thing that is different from three months ago, and what is the next step?" — and if the loop continues, close the feed rather than feeding it new targets.

If you repeat one small version of these steps daily — name it, cut the passive dose, test the target, take one step — expect it to become easier slowly, not this week. In the habit research this guide cites throughout, Lally and colleagues (2010) found that a new daily behaviour took a median of 66 days to become automatic, with a wide range of 18 to 254 days, and that missing a single day did not materially affect the process. A bad comparison day is not a failed system. It is one day.

## Where do apps fit in this?

An affirmation app cannot unfollow anyone for you, change what a feed shows you, or give you the years another person's outcome took. What it can do, at most, is put a believable sentence in front of you in the minute after a comparison lands, before the rumination starts — a sentence sized to your actual next step, not to someone else's highlight. Used that way, it belongs after Step 1: name the comparison, read one card, then do the step from Step 4. Used as another feed to scroll while you feel behind, it becomes one more passive surface, and Verduyn and colleagues' (2015) result predicts what that will cost.

What to check before you rely on any app for this: whether you can choose the struggle you are in (overthinking, self-criticism, a hard day) rather than receiving the same generic lines as everyone else; whether the words are sized to be believed on a bad day — "I can take the next step" rather than "I am the best"; whether it reaches you during the day, when the comparisons happen, instead of only when you remember to open it; and what it costs, in full, after any trial. Anicca is built around those choices: you pick the struggles, and short cards on those topics arrive through the day. That is a design claim, not a result. The measured part is the next section.

## Our own numbers, printed as they are

Anicca is small, and we publish the smallness. When we checked in November 2026, its US App Store listing showed 5.0 stars from 1 rating, and its Japanese listing 4.5 stars from 48 ratings. App Store Connect recorded 1 first download for Anicca in the 7 days to 12 November 2026. Premium is $59.99 a year on the US listing. Notice what this section is doing: it is the comparison discipline of this guide applied to us. If social proof is what you need — and for something you open on the days you feel behind, it is a reasonable thing to need — larger apps have it and we do not, yet. What we can claim is only the design: a short card, on the topic you chose, arriving while the day is happening — not another person's timeline arriving with it.

## When is comparing yourself a sign to get human help?

If comparison is there most days, if you are avoiding work, friends or opportunities because you expect to fall short, if your sleep is broken by rumination about where you stand, or if your mood stays low for weeks, treat that as a reason to talk to a clinician or a counsellor, not to download more software. Constant painful comparison can be part of depression, social anxiety, an eating disorder or body-image difficulties, low self-esteem that has become entrenched, or a life situation — debt, an unsafe workplace, a relationship that measures you — that deserves its own support. If the measuring itself is the harm in your daily life, help with that is the treatment-shaped answer. If you ever feel that you might act on thoughts of harming yourself, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line in your country now — in Japan, call 110 or 119 in an emergency; in the US, call or text 988. An article — including this one — is information, not assessment, and it is not a verdict on your worth.

## Common questions

### Why do I compare myself even when I know the post is edited?

Because knowing and measuring are different operations. Festinger (1954) described comparison as the fallback when no objective standard is at hand, and a feed puts a vivid, specific target in front of you at the exact moment you have no objective record open. The knowledge "this is edited" is general; the image is specific, and specific targets are what the comparison system uses. That is why Step 2 works on exposure and mode (Verduyn et al., 2015) rather than asking you to believe harder that the post is not real.

### Why does someone else's success sometimes motivate me and sometimes crush me?

The research gives two switches. The first is attainability and relevance: Lockwood and Kunda (1997) found role models inspired when their success seemed relevant and attainable, and deflated when it seemed out of reach. The second is the kind of envy: Van de Ven and colleagues (2009, 2011) distinguish benign envy, which aims at improving your own position and motivated self-improvement in their studies, from malicious envy, which aims at pulling the other down and motivated no improvement. Same post, different settings. Steps 3 and 4 are built to set them deliberately.

### Should I compare myself downward, to people doing worse, to feel better?

It can lift a self-evaluation briefly — Vogel and colleagues (2014) found state self-esteem was higher after a downward-comparison profile than after an upward one — but this guide does not recommend it as a practice. It keeps the same measurement error, just pointed the other way: your worth still rises and falls with whoever you looked at last, and it trains the habit Gibbons and Buunk (1999) measured, in which frequent comparers feel comparisons more strongly. The fair comparison in Step 5 — your own record — does the steadying job without needing anyone to be below you.

### Why do I compare the most at night and when I am already tired?

Partly because that is when the feeds are open and the objective record is closed, and partly because of what comparison starts. Feinstein and colleagues (2013) found negative Facebook comparison predicted increases in rumination over 3 weeks in 268 young adults, and rumination is a night-time process: there is no next task to compete with it. Gibbons and Buunk (1999) add that high comparison orientation travels with self-uncertainty and negative affectivity, both of which are louder when you are depleted. The practical answer is Steps 2 and 5 done before bed: no passive feed in the last hour, and the one fair comparison — against your own record — already written down.

### How long should I try these steps before judging whether they help?

Judge them on whether the sting gets shorter and the rumination gets quieter over two to three weeks of most days — not on one evening next to someone's announcement. For the habit underneath them, Lally and colleagues (2010) measured a median of 66 days for a new daily behaviour to become automatic, ranging from 18 to 254 days, with a single missed day making no material difference. If weeks of trying leave you avoiding more of your life, or the mood stays low, that is information for the "get human help" section above, not a verdict on your effort.

### Can an affirmation app stop me comparing myself to others?

No. An app cannot change your feed, your comparison orientation, or the years behind another person's outcome, and any app that promises to stop comparison is claiming more than the evidence in this guide supports — the meta-analytic average effect of upward comparison itself was small (g = −0.24; McComb et al., 2023), and no app study in this guide measured an app removing it. What an app can do is small and specific: put one believable sentence in front of you in the minute after a comparison, so that Step 4 — one copyable step — is easier to begin. If it does that, it has done its whole job.
